title: Life Cycles and Traits
bigQuestion: Why do living things look like their parents, but never exactly the same?

story.title: The Monarchs of Room 12
story.kicker: A jar of milkweed leaves, five tiny eggs, and a class that learned to wait.
paragraphs: In September, Ms. Ortiz brought a jar of milkweed leaves into Room 12. On the bottom of one leaf were five eggs. Each egg was smaller than the head of a pin. It was pale yellow and shaped like a tiny football. The class put the jar by the window and started a chart. Day 1: five eggs. Nothing else to report.

On Day 4, a student named Jamal shouted. One egg had a hole in it. A caterpillar the size of a grain of rice was chewing its way out. Then it did something strange. It ate its own eggshell. Over the next two weeks, the caterpillars ate and ate. They grew striped in yellow, black and white. Each one shed its skin four times, like a jacket that got too tight.

On Day 18, the biggest caterpillar climbed to the lid of the jar. It hung upside down in the shape of the letter J. The next morning it was gone. In its place hung a smooth green case with gold dots. It looked like a jewel. The class called it a chrysalis. For ten days it did not seem to move at all. Some students thought it had died.

On Day 29, the green case turned dark. Then it turned clear. Through the shell the class could see orange and black wings folded up tight. At 10:15 that morning the shell split. A wet, crumpled butterfly crawled out. It hung still while its wings filled out and dried. By lunch, it was a monarch, the state insect of Illinois.

Two of the five butterflies had a small black spot on each back wing. Ms. Ortiz explained that those two were males. All five had the same orange and black pattern as their parents, who the class had never seen. But no two were exactly the same size. On a sunny afternoon the class let them go in the school garden. It was late September. Those monarchs were about to fly roughly 2,000 miles to the mountains of Mexico.
story.think: The class never saw the parents of these butterflies. How could they still know what the parents looked like?

lessons.title: The Same Four Stages
lessons.mainIdea: Every living thing is born, grows, may reproduce, and dies, and the cycle starts again with the next generation.
reading: A puppy is born. It grows into a dog. That dog may have puppies of its own. Someday the dog dies. Its puppies grow up and have puppies. This pattern is called a *life cycle*. Every kind of living thing has one. A sunflower has one. A frog has one. So do you.

All life cycles share the same big stages. First comes birth, which for many living things means hatching or sprouting. Then comes growth. Next, an adult may *reproduce*, which means making new living things like itself. Last comes death. The cycle does not end there, because the young ones carry it on.

The stages are the same, but the details are wildly different. A mayfly may live as an adult for only a day. A bur oak can stand for 300 years. Some animals are born looking like tiny adults. Others, like frogs, change shape completely. Scientists compare life cycles to find what all living things have in common.

words.d: the stages a living thing goes through: birth, growth, reproduction and death
to make new living things of the same kind

look.title: The Class Pet's Story
look.text: Room 12 also has a class hamster named Biscuit. Biscuit was born in a pet store in the spring. She is now full grown and about the size of a tennis ball. Hamsters usually live about two to three years. Some hamsters have a litter of six or more babies.
look.prompt: Which stages of the life cycle has Biscuit already gone through? Which have not happened yet?

check.q: What do all life cycles have in common?
check.why: Every living thing is born, grows, may reproduce and dies. Hatching, changing shape and long life happen only for some kinds.

check.q: A mayfly and a bur oak both have life cycles. Which sentence is true?
choices: Only the oak really has a life cycle
Both have the same stages, but the stages last very different times
Both live about the same number of years
The mayfly skips the growth stage
check.why: Both go through birth, growth, reproduction and death. A mayfly adult may live a day; an oak may live 300 years.

check.q: Why does a life cycle not end when one animal dies?
choices: Because its young carry on the cycle
Because the cycle only has three stages
check.why: The animal's offspring are born, grow and reproduce, so the cycle continues with the next generation.

lessons.title: A Frog Changes Shape
lessons.mainIdea: A frog starts as an egg in water, lives as a tadpole with gills and a tail, and slowly changes into an air-breathing adult.
reading: In April, an Illinois pond is full of frog eggs. Each egg is a black dot inside a ball of clear jelly. The eggs float in clumps near the shore. After one to three weeks, tiny *tadpoles* wiggle out. A tadpole does not look like a frog at all. It has a round body, a long tail and no legs. It breathes water through *gills*, like a fish.

The tadpole eats and grows. Then the changes begin. Two back legs sprout. Then two front legs appear. Lungs grow inside its body. The tail gets shorter and shorter. It is not cut off. The body slowly takes the tail back in and uses it as food. Finally, a small frog with no tail hops onto the shore and breathes air.

This big change in body shape is called *metamorphosis*. The word means change of form. How long it takes depends on the kind of frog. A spring peeper can finish in a couple of months. A bullfrog tadpole may stay in the water through a whole winter. The adult frog lays eggs in the pond, and the cycle starts again.

words.d: the young stage of a frog, which lives in water and has a tail and gills
body parts that take oxygen out of water, used by fish and tadpoles
a big change in body shape as a young animal becomes an adult

look.title: Two Photos From the Pond
look.text: Look at two pictures taken at the same pond. In the first, from May, the shallow water is crowded with black tadpoles the size of jelly beans. In the second, from August, there are no tadpoles. Small frogs sit along the muddy edge, and a few still have a stub of a tail.
look.prompt: What happened between May and August? What does the stub of a tail tell you?

check.q: How does a tadpole breathe?
choices: With lungs, like an adult frog
It does not need to breathe
check.why: A tadpole lives in water and takes oxygen from the water with gills. Lungs grow later, during metamorphosis.

check.q: What happens to a tadpole's tail?
choices: It falls off in one piece
The body slowly takes it back in
It grows into the back legs
It stays on the adult frog
check.why: The tail is not cut off. The body slowly absorbs it and uses it as food while the frog finishes changing.

check.q: Which change would you expect to see FIRST as a tadpole becomes a frog?
check.why: The back legs appear first. The front legs come next, the tail shrinks, and only then does the frog leave the water.

lessons.title: A Butterfly's Four Stages
lessons.mainIdea: A monarch passes through four stages, egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult, and each stage has a different job.
reading: A monarch has four stages. It starts as an egg the size of a pinhead. A female lays each egg on a *milkweed* leaf. Only milkweed will do, because monarch caterpillars eat nothing else. In about four days, a caterpillar chews its way out. The caterpillar's job is simple: eat. In about two weeks it grows roughly 2,000 times heavier than when it hatched.

Next the caterpillar hangs upside down and sheds its skin one last time. Underneath is a smooth green case called a *chrysalis*. Inside, the insect's body is being rebuilt. Wings, long legs and a coiled drinking tube take shape. Nothing seems to happen on the outside. Inside, almost everything is changing.

After about ten days, the case splits and an adult butterfly climbs out. The adult's job is different from the caterpillar's job. It drinks *nectar* from flowers, finds a mate and lays eggs. It cannot chew leaves at all. Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult: this is one full turn of the monarch's life cycle.

words.d: a wild plant with milky sap; the only food monarch caterpillars eat
the hard case a caterpillar forms while it changes into a butterfly
the sweet liquid inside flowers that butterflies and bees drink

look.title: How Long Each Monarch Stage Lasts
look.cite: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service monarch pages, rounded
look.prompt: About how many days pass from egg to adult? Which stage is longest?

check.q: Where does a monarch lay her eggs?
check.why: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, so the female lays each egg on a milkweed leaf.

check.q: What is happening inside the chrysalis?
choices: The insect is resting and nothing changes
The caterpillar is eating stored leaves
The body is being rebuilt into a butterfly
check.why: The outside looks still, but inside the body is being rebuilt with wings, long legs and a drinking tube.

check.q: Using the data, about how many days does it take to go from egg to adult butterfly?
check.why: Add the egg, caterpillar and chrysalis stages: 4 + 12 + 10 = 26 days, about four weeks.

lessons.title: A Bean and an Oak
lessons.mainIdea: Plants have life cycles too: a seed sprouts, grows, makes flowers and seeds, and dies, quickly for a bean and slowly for an oak.
reading: Put a bean seed in a wet paper towel. In two or three days the seed swells and splits. A white root pokes out and heads down. A pale shoot heads up. This is *germination*, the sprouting of a seed. The seed's food is stored inside it, so the plant can grow before it has leaves.

A bean plant grows fast. In a few weeks it has leaves and flowers. Each flower turns into a pod. Inside the pod are new bean seeds. By fall, the bean plant dies. The whole cycle takes one summer. But its seeds can wait in the soil and sprout next spring.

An oak starts the same way, from a seed called an *acorn*. But an oak does not hurry. It may grow 20 years or more before it makes its first acorns. A white oak, the state tree of Illinois, can live for several hundred years. Same stages: seed, *seedling*, adult, seeds. Very different clock.

words.d: the sprouting of a seed, when the root and shoot first grow out
the seed of an oak tree
a young plant that has just sprouted from a seed

look.title: The Bean Journal
look.text: Day 1: seed is hard and white. Day 3: seed is fat and the coat is split; a root 1 cm long. Day 5: root 4 cm, shoot bent like a hook. Day 7: shoot straight, two leaves open, green. Day 14: plant 15 cm tall, four leaves.
look.prompt: What grew first, the root or the shoot? Why might that be useful for the plant?

check.q: What comes out of a bean seed first?
check.why: The root comes out first and heads down to find water. The shoot and leaves follow.

check.q: How is an oak's life cycle different from a bean's?
choices: An oak does not make seeds
An oak takes many years for each stage; a bean takes one summer
A bean lives longer than an oak
check.why: Both have the same stages, but a bean finishes in one summer while an oak may take 20 years just to make its first acorns.

check.q: Where does a sprouting bean get food before it has leaves?
choices: From food stored inside the seed
check.why: Food is stored inside the seed. That is why a bean can sprout on a paper towel with no soil.

lessons.title: What a Trait Is
lessons.mainIdea: A trait is a feature of a living thing, and many traits are inherited, passed from parents to their young.
reading: Look at your hand. Your fingers, your skin color, the shape of your thumbnail: each is a *trait*. A trait is a feature a living thing has. Eye color is a trait. A cat's stripes are a trait. A pea plant's flower color is a trait. Traits can be seen, or measured, or both.

Many traits are *inherited*. That means they are passed from parents to *offspring*. A calico cat's kittens are often calico. Two tall parents usually have tall children. Monarchs are orange and black because their parents were. The instructions for these traits are inside every living thing, and a copy goes to each of the young.

Farmers have known about inherited traits for thousands of years. They saved seeds from the sweetest corn. They bred the cows that gave the most milk. In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel counted thousands of pea plants. He showed that traits pass from parents to offspring in patterns you can predict.

words.d: a feature of a living thing, such as eye color or leaf shape
passed from parents to their young
the young of a living thing; its children

look.title: Mendel Counts His Peas
look.text: In his 1866 paper, Mendel explained that he had grown and counted pea plants for eight years. He crossed plants with round seeds and plants with wrinkled seeds. He reported that the first generation all had round seeds, and that in the next generation about three plants in four had round seeds and one in four had wrinkled seeds.
look.cite: Gregor Mendel, Experiments on Plant Hybrids, 1866 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why did Mendel count so many plants instead of just a few?

check.q: Which of these is an inherited trait?
check.why: Eye color is passed from parents. A scar, a language and a favorite song all come from what happens during your life.

check.q: What does 'inherited' mean?
check.why: An inherited trait comes from the parents. It is not learned, chosen or caused by the weather.

check.q: Mendel crossed round-seed peas with wrinkled-seed peas. In the first generation, what did he see?
check.why: The first generation all had round seeds. Wrinkled seeds showed up again only in the next generation, about one in four.

lessons.title: Why Brothers and Sisters Differ
lessons.mainIdea: Offspring get traits from both parents, so brothers and sisters are alike in many ways but never exactly the same.
reading: A litter of puppies is born. Same mother, same father, same day. Yet one puppy is brown, one is black, and one has a white paw. One grows bigger than the rest. This is *variation*. It means members of a family, or of a kind, are different from one another.

Variation happens because each young one gets traits from both parents. The mix is a little different every time. One puppy may get its mother's ears and its father's color. Another may get the reverse. Only *identical* twins start with the same instructions. Even they can end up a bit different.

Variation is easy to see if you look closely. Pick up ten acorns from one white oak. Measure them. Some are long, some are round, some have thick caps. Look at monarchs from the same egg batch. Some have wider black lines. Charles Darwin noticed that no two members of a kind are ever exactly alike. That idea became one of the most important in all of science.

words.d: the differences among members of one family or one kind of living thing
exactly the same

look.title: Darwin's Last Sentence
look.text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859 (last sentence of the first edition)
look.prompt: Darwin says forms of life 'are being' made, not just 'have been.' What do you think he means?

check.q: Puppies in one litter have different colors. What is this called?
check.why: Variation means the members of a family or kind differ from one another, even with the same parents.

check.q: Why are brothers and sisters not exactly the same?
choices: Each gets a different mix of traits from both parents
Only the oldest child inherits traits
Traits are picked at random from strangers
check.why: Each child gets traits from both parents, but the mix is a little different every time.

check.q: You measure ten acorns from one tree. What would you predict?
choices: All ten are exactly the same size
They are all different kinds of seed
Most will be similar, but none will be exactly alike
check.why: Acorns from one tree share many traits, but variation means no two are exactly the same.

lessons.title: The World Shapes Traits Too
lessons.mainIdea: Some traits are changed by the environment, by food, sunlight, weather and experience, not only by what parents pass on.
reading: Grow two bean plants from seeds off the same pod. Put one in a sunny window. Put the other in a dark closet. In a week, the sunny plant is short, green and sturdy. The closet plant is tall, thin and yellow-white. Same parents, same instructions, very different plants. The difference came from the *environment*, everything around the plant.

Animals are shaped by their environment too. A well-fed dog grows bigger than its hungry brother. A flamingo is pink only if it eats pink shrimp and algae. Without them, its feathers turn pale. Your skin gets darker in summer sun. Muscles grow when you use them. A scar comes from a cut. None of these were passed on by parents. They are *acquired traits*, picked up during life.

Some traits come from both. Height is inherited, but a child with poor food may not reach it. The language you speak is not inherited at all. You learned it from the people around you. Scientists ask a careful question about every trait: how much comes from the parents, and how much from the world?

words.d: everything around a living thing: light, water, food, weather and other living things
a feature a living thing gets from its surroundings or experience, not from its parents

look.title: Hydrangeas on Two Sides of the Street
look.text: On Maple Street, two neighbors planted cuttings from the same hydrangea bush. Cuttings are pieces of one plant, so they carry the same instructions. One yard has sour, acid soil. Its flowers came out blue. The other yard has sweeter, chalky soil. Its flowers came out pink.
look.prompt: The plants have the same instructions. Why are the flowers different colors? Is flower color inherited, acquired, or both?

check.q: Two bean plants from the same pod grow differently in sun and in a closet. What caused the difference?
check.why: The seeds came from the same pod and are the same age. Light, part of the environment, made the difference.

check.q: Which trait is acquired, not inherited?
check.why: A scar comes from something that happened during life. Hair color, finger number and earlobe shape are inherited.

check.q: A flamingo stops eating pink shrimp and algae. What would you predict?
choices: Its feathers stay bright pink forever
check.why: The pink color comes from the food. Without it, new feathers grow in pale.

lessons.title: Traits That Help Find Food
lessons.mainIdea: Some traits give an individual an advantage in finding food, so that individual is more likely to survive and reproduce.
reading: Two great blue herons stand in a Chicago lagoon. One has slightly longer legs. It can wade into deeper water where more fish hide. It eats more. It stays stronger through the winter. A trait that helps a living thing survive is called an *advantage*. Long legs are an advantage for a heron. They would be no help to a mole.

Look at a bird's beak and you can often guess its food. A cardinal's thick beak cracks seeds. A woodpecker's chisel beak digs insects out of bark. A hummingbird's needle beak reaches nectar deep in flowers. Among woodpeckers, the ones with slightly stronger beaks may find more food in a hard winter.

Color can be an advantage too. A brown moth resting on brown bark is hard for a bird to see. This is *camouflage*, blending in. A white moth on the same bark stands out. The brown moth is more likely to live and have young. Its young are more likely to be brown. Over many generations, advantages like this add up.

words.d: a trait that helps a living thing survive or reproduce better than others of its kind
colors or patterns that help a living thing blend in with its surroundings

look.title: Winter at the Feeder
look.text: A backyard feeder in Peoria is filled with sunflower seeds. Cardinals crack the seeds easily with their thick beaks. A robin lands, pecks at a seed, and gives up. Robins have thin beaks made for pulling worms from soil. In January, the ground is frozen hard.
look.prompt: Which bird has the advantage at this feeder in January? What could happen to the robin?

check.q: Which beak is best for cracking hard seeds?
check.why: A thick, short beak, like a cardinal's, can squeeze hard enough to crack a seed.

check.q: A brown moth and a white moth rest on brown bark. Which is more likely to survive, and why?
choices: The white moth, because it is easier to see
The brown moth, because birds see it more easily
The brown moth, because it blends in and birds miss it
Both the same, because color does not matter
check.why: Camouflage hides the brown moth from birds. The white moth stands out and is more likely to be eaten.

check.q: Why do advantages 'add up' over many generations?
choices: Because the young of survivors often inherit the helpful trait
Because animals choose their traits each spring
Because all animals in a kind are identical
check.why: Survivors have young, and the young often inherit the trait. So each generation has more individuals with it.

lessons.title: Traits That Help Find a Mate
lessons.mainIdea: Some traits help an animal attract a mate, so that animal is more likely to reproduce and pass those traits on.
reading: A male cardinal in February is the reddest thing in a gray Illinois yard. That color costs him. Hawks can see him from far away. So why is he red? Female cardinals tend to choose brighter males to *mate* with. A bright male has more young. His sons tend to be bright too. The trait keeps going.

Sound works the same way. On a spring night, male frogs call from every pond. Each kind has its own call. Females move toward the loudest, clearest callers. On a summer night, male fireflies flash a code. A female that likes the pattern flashes back. Every song and flash is a way of saying, choose me.

The peacock's tail is the famous example. It is heavy and hard to hide. But peahens choose the males with the biggest, brightest tails. Darwin puzzled over this. A trait can be a burden for survival and still spread, if it helps an animal win a mate. Scientists call this *sexual selection*.

words.d: to pair up and reproduce; also, the partner an animal pairs with
when a trait spreads because it helps an animal attract a mate

look.title: The Feather That Made Darwin Sick
look.text: In an 1860 letter to a friend, Darwin joked that the sight of a feather in a peacock's tail made him feel sick whenever he looked at it. He could not yet explain how such a heavy, showy trait, which made the bird easier to catch, could exist. Later he argued that the tail spread because peahens preferred it.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, letter to Asa Gray, 1860 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why would a peacock's tail bother Darwin? What idea did he later use to explain it?

check.q: Why are male cardinals bright red even though hawks can see them?
choices: Females tend to choose brighter males, so bright males have more young
Red helps them hide in snow
check.why: Bright males win more mates and have more young, so the trait is passed on even though it has a cost.

check.q: How does a female firefly choose a mate?
check.why: Male fireflies flash a code. A female that likes the pattern flashes back.

check.q: A peacock's tail makes it slower to escape a fox. Why does the trait still spread?
choices: The tail also helps it fly faster
Peahens choose big-tailed males, so those males have more young
check.why: A trait can hurt survival and still spread if it helps win a mate. That is sexual selection.

lessons.title: Comparing Life Spans
lessons.mainIdea: Life cycles share the same stages, but the length of a life and of each stage varies enormously from one kind of living thing to another.
reading: How long is a life? For a monarch that hatches in June, about a month as a caterpillar and chrysalis, then a few weeks as an adult. For a monarch that hatches in late summer, much longer. That one flies to Mexico, rests all winter, and lives about eight months. Same kind of butterfly, very different *life span*.

Scientists measure life spans by tagging and counting. They put a tiny sticker, a *tag*, on a monarch's wing. They band birds' legs. They count *tree rings* in a stump; each ring is one year. A house mouse usually lives about two years. A dog, about twelve. A horse, close to thirty. A bur oak in an Illinois prairie can pass 300 years.

A long life is not always an advantage. A mouse lives a short life but can have several litters a year. An oak lives long but may not make acorns for twenty years. Each way of living has worked for a very long time. Comparing life cycles shows there is no single best way to be alive.

words.d: how long a living thing usually lives, from birth to death
a small marker put on an animal so scientists can track it
the layers of wood a tree adds each year, seen as rings in a cut trunk

look.title: Typical Life Spans
look.prompt: Which living thing on the list lives longest? About how many mouse lives fit in one dog life?

check.q: How can you tell the age of a cut tree?
choices: Count the rings in the trunk
check.why: A tree adds one ring of wood each year, so counting rings gives its age.

check.q: Using the data, about how many times longer does a horse live than a house mouse?
check.why: A horse lives about 28 years and a mouse about 2. 28 divided by 2 is 14.

check.q: A monarch that hatches in late summer lives much longer than one that hatches in June. What is the best explanation?
choices: The late-summer monarch migrates to Mexico and rests through the winter
It is a different kind of butterfly
June monarchs are eaten by birds
check.why: The late-summer generation flies south and rests all winter, living about eight months instead of a few weeks.

review.q: Which list shows the stages of a monarch's life cycle in order?
review.why: A monarch starts as an egg, hatches into a caterpillar, forms a chrysalis, and comes out as an adult.

review.q: A tadpole and an adult frog look very different. What is this change called?
review.why: Metamorphosis means a big change of body form as a young animal becomes an adult.

review.q: Which is the best example of an inherited trait?
choices: A bean plant that is pale from growing in a closet
A dog that is fat from too much food
A kitten with the same striped fur as its mother
A student who learned to speak Spanish
review.why: The kitten's stripes were passed from its mother. The others came from food, light or learning.

review.q: Two puppies in one litter have different colors. Why?
choices: Each got a different mix of traits from its two parents
review.why: Each puppy inherits traits from both parents, but the mix is different for each one. That is variation.
An acorn is the seed of an oak. When it germinates, it becomes an oak seedling.

review.q: A heron with longer legs can wade deeper and catch more fish. What is this trait an example of?
review.why: Longer legs help the heron get more food, so the trait is an advantage.

review.q: Male frogs call loudly on spring nights. What is the main purpose of the call?
review.why: Females move toward the loudest, clearest callers. The call helps a male win a mate.

review.q: A bean plant grown in a dark closet is tall, thin and pale. Its sibling in the sun is short and green. What caused the difference?
review.why: The plants came from the same pod. The difference in light, part of the environment, changed how they grew.
